title: Units and Measurement
description: Scientists use standard units to measure time, distance, mass, and volume. Using standard units lets scientists share and compare measurements accurately.

exercises.question: Which unit is BEST for measuring the time it takes to run a 100 m race?
exercises.exp: A 100 m race takes about 10–20 seconds! Seconds are perfect for measuring short events.

exercises.question: Which unit is BEST for measuring the distance from your house to school?
exercises.exp: Kilometres are best for longer distances — a typical school is 1–5 km from home.

exercises.question: Which is the correct abbreviation for METRES?
exercises.exp: m is the abbreviation for metres. 1 metre = 100 centimetres = 1000 millimetres.

exercises.question: Which is the correct abbreviation for GRAMS?
exercises.exp: g is the abbreviation for grams. 1000 grams = 1 kilogram (kg).

exercises.question: How many seconds are in ONE MINUTE?
exercises.exp: 60 seconds = 1 minute. 60 minutes = 1 hour. 24 hours = 1 day.

exercises.question: A science experiment takes 2.5 hours. How many MINUTES is this?
exercises.exp: 2.5 hours × 60 minutes/hour = 150 minutes. Always multiply hours by 60 to get minutes!

exercises.question: Which unit measures VOLUME of liquid?
exercises.exp: Millilitres (mL) and litres (L) measure volume of liquid. 1000 mL = 1 L.

exercises.question: A water bottle holds 500 mL. How many LITRES is this?
exercises.exp: 500 mL ÷ 1000 = 0.5 L. Half a litre fits in a standard water bottle!

exercises.question: Which is the LONGEST unit of time in this list?
exercises.exp: A day (24 hours) is longest. 1 day > 1 hour > 1 minute > 1 second.

exercises.question: A rock has a MASS of 2.5 kg. How many GRAMS is this?
exercises.exp: 2.5 kg × 1000 g/kg = 2500 g. Multiply kilograms by 1000 to convert to grams.

exercises.question: Why is it important to use STANDARD UNITS in science?
choices: to make experiments look more official
so everyone can understand and compare measurements accurately
exercises.exp: Standard units (like metres and kilograms) mean scientists worldwide can share results and compare measurements accurately.

exercises.question: Which abbreviation is used for KILOMETRES?
exercises.exp: km is the correct abbreviation for kilometre. Only the k is lowercase. 1 km = 1000 metres.

exercises.question: How many millimetres are in 1 CENTIMETRE?
exercises.exp: 10 mm = 1 cm. Milli means 'one thousandth' of a metre (0.001 m). Centi means 'one hundredth' of a metre (0.01 m).

exercises.question: How many centimetres are in 1 METRE?
exercises.exp: 100 cm = 1 m. Centi = 1/100. So 1 m = 100 centimetres.

exercises.question: How many metres are in 1 KILOMETRE?
exercises.exp: 1000 m = 1 km. Kilo always means one thousand. So 1 kilometre = 1000 metres.

exercises.question: A desk is 75 cm wide. How many MILLIMETRES is that?
exercises.exp: 1 cm = 10 mm. So 75 cm × 10 = 750 mm.

exercises.question: A marathon race is 42.195 km. How many METRES is this?
What is 3.5 kg in GRAMS?
A medicine bottle contains 250 mL. How many LITRES is this?
How many SECONDS are in 1 HOUR?
exercises.exp: 1 hour = 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 3600 seconds.

exercises.question: A scientist records 2 hours 15 minutes of observations. How many MINUTES total?
exercises.exp: 2 hours × 60 = 120 minutes + 15 minutes = 135 minutes total.

exercises.question: Which metric PREFIX means 'one thousandth' (0.001)?
exercises.exp: Milli (m) = 0.001. So 1 millimetre = 0.001 m. 1 milligram = 0.001 g. 1 millisecond = 0.001 s.

exercises.question: Which metric PREFIX means 'one thousand' (1000)?
exercises.exp: Kilo (k) = 1000. So 1 kilogram = 1000 g. 1 kilometre = 1000 m. 1 kilolitre = 1000 L.

exercises.question: A recipe needs 1.5 L of stock. The cook only has a 250 mL measuring cup. How many CUPS are needed?
A student measures a caterpillar as 32 mm. A classmate says it is 3.2 cm. Are they both CORRECT?
choices: no — they measured differently so one must be wrong
yes — 32 mm = 3.2 cm (just different units for the same length)
no — you must use mm for small objects
yes — they are close but not equal
exercises.exp: 1 cm = 10 mm. So 32 mm ÷ 10 = 3.2 cm. Same measurement, different units — both are correct!

exercises.question: Why do scientists use METRIC (SI) units instead of imperial units (inches, pounds)?
choices: imperial units are harder to learn
metric units are based on multiples of 10 — easy to convert, and universally used in science worldwide for consistent communication
metric units are newer and better looking
scientists are required to use metric by law in all countries
exercises.exp: The metric system's base-10 structure makes conversions simple (multiply/divide by 10, 100, 1000). It is used by virtually all scientists worldwide, allowing clear global communication of results.

exercises.question: Which measurement tool would BEST measure the mass of a small rock?
choices: a balance scale or digital scale (in grams)
exercises.exp: Mass is measured with a balance or digital scale — in grams for small objects or kilograms for larger ones. Rulers measure length; cups measure volume.

exercises.question: A clock shows it is 2:45 pm. School ends at 3:30 pm. How many MINUTES until school ends?
exercises.exp: From 2:45 to 3:00 = 15 minutes. From 3:00 to 3:30 = 30 minutes. Total = 15 + 30 = 45 minutes.

exercises.question: An experiment measures temperature change: starts at 18°C and ends at 31°C. What is the CHANGE in temperature?
exercises.exp: Temperature change = final − initial = 31°C − 18°C = 13°C increase.

exercises.question: A student makes THREE measurements of the same object: 14.2 cm, 14.3 cm, 14.1 cm. What is the AVERAGE measurement?
exercises.exp: Average = (14.2 + 14.3 + 14.1) ÷ 3 = 42.6 ÷ 3 = 14.2 cm. Averaging multiple measurements gives a more reliable result!

exercises.question: Which is the MOST PRECISE measurement?
exercises.exp: Precision = number of decimal places and significant figures. 4.82 cm (2 decimal places) is most precise — it gives the most detailed information about the length.

exercises.question: You need 2.75 kg of flour. The scale reads in grams. What number should you read on the scale?
exercises.exp: 2.75 kg × 1000 g/kg = 2750 g. When the scale reads 2750, you have exactly 2.75 kilograms of flour.

exercises.question: Which set of measurement tools would a scientist use for a complete experiment?
choices: thermometer, ruler, scale, measuring cylinder — each for a different measurable quantity
just a calculator, no measuring tools needed
exercises.exp: Different quantities need different tools: length → ruler; temperature → thermometer; mass → scale; volume → measuring cylinder. Scientists choose the right tool for each measurement!

exercises.question: SIGNIFICANT FIGURES indicate ___.
choices: the number of meaningful digits in a measurement that reflect its precision
only the digits after the decimal point
the number of zeros in a measurement
exercises.exp: Significant figures show precision. '4.82 cm' has 3 sig figs (more precise); '5 cm' has 1 sig fig (less precise). Scientists report sig figs to show measurement uncertainty.

exercises.question: What is ACCURACY in measurement?
choices: how many decimal places a reading has
how close a measurement is to the true/accepted value
how consistent repeated measurements are with each other
how fast the measurement was taken
exercises.exp: Accuracy: closeness to the true value. If the true temperature is 37.0°C and you measure 37.1°C — very accurate! Many decimal places does not mean accurate if the instrument is faulty.

exercises.question: What is PRECISION in measurement?
choices: how close a measurement is to the true value
how consistent repeated measurements are with each other (reproducibility)
how expensive the measuring tool is
the smallest unit on the scale
exercises.exp: Precision: consistency of repeated readings. You can be precise but inaccurate (consistently wrong). You can be accurate but imprecise (close on average but variable). Best = both accurate AND precise!

exercises.question: A scientist measures the same object FIVE TIMES and gets: 4.8, 4.9, 4.8, 4.8, 4.9 cm. These readings are ___.
choices: precise (consistent with each other) but accuracy depends on the true value
exercises.exp: These readings are PRECISE — they cluster closely together. Whether they are accurate depends on whether the true value is ~4.8-4.9 cm. Precision is about consistency.

exercises.question: To find the VOLUME of a small irregular solid object (like a pebble), you can use ___.
choices: only a ruler — measure all sides
water displacement — place in a measuring cylinder and measure how much the water level rises
no method works for irregular shapes
exercises.exp: Archimedes' method: submerge the object in water — the rise in water level equals the object's volume. Volume of water displaced = volume of irregular solid. Brilliant!

exercises.question: The MENISCUS is the curve formed when liquid is in a glass tube. Scientists read liquid volume at ___.
choices: the highest point of the curved surface
the lowest point of the curved surface (bottom of meniscus) for most liquids like water
the top of the tube edge
exercises.exp: Water (and most liquids) form a concave meniscus — the bottom of the curve is the true liquid level. Always read at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus for accuracy!

exercises.question: PARALLAX ERROR in measurement occurs when ___.
choices: you read a scale from an angle instead of directly head-on, causing an incorrect reading
you use the wrong type of measuring tool
exercises.exp: Parallax error: reading a scale at an angle makes the reading appear higher or lower. Always read scales at eye level, perpendicular to the scale, to avoid parallax error!

exercises.question: Converting 85 mm to centimetres gives ___.
exercises.exp: 1 cm = 10 mm, so mm ÷ 10 = cm. 85 ÷ 10 = 8.5 cm. Move the decimal one place left when dividing by 10!

exercises.question: A car travels 240 km in 3 hours. What is its average speed?
exercises.exp: Speed = Distance ÷ Time = 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h. If it maintains this average, it covers 80 kilometres every hour!

exercises.question: DENSITY = mass ÷ volume. A rock has a mass of 150 g and volume of 50 cm³. What is its density?
exercises.exp: Density = mass ÷ volume = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 g/cm³. Water is 1 g/cm³, so this rock (3 g/cm³) is 3 times denser than water — it would sink!

exercises.question: A thermometer reads −5°C on a cold morning and +18°C in the afternoon. What is the temperature CHANGE?
exercises.exp: Temperature change = final − initial = 18 − (−5) = 18 + 5 = 23°C. Subtracting a negative number means adding — the temperature rose by 23°C!

exercises.question: Which is GREATER: 2.5 litres or 2450 millilitres?
choices: 2450 mL — 2.5 L = 2500 mL > 2450 mL, so 2.5 L is greater
exercises.exp: Convert: 2.5 L = 2500 mL. Compare: 2500 mL > 2450 mL. So 2.5 litres is GREATER than 2450 mL by 50 mL!

exercises.question: What is the PERIMETER of a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide?
exercises.exp: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 cm. Perimeter is the total distance around the outside of the shape!

exercises.question: What is the AREA of a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide?
exercises.exp: Area = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Area measures the surface inside a shape — in square centimetres. Perimeter goes AROUND; area fills IN.

exercises.question: The SI unit of time is the ___.
exercises.exp: The SI unit of time is the second (s). All other time units are multiples: 60 s = 1 minute; 3600 s = 1 hour. Scientific calculations use seconds!

exercises.question: An experiment measures plant growth every day. The INDEPENDENT variable (what the scientist changes) is ___.
choices: the height of the plant (what is measured)
the number of days (time — the scientist controls when measurements are taken)
exercises.exp: Independent variable = what the scientist deliberately changes or controls. Here, time (days) is controlled — the scientist decides when to measure.

exercises.question: The DEPENDENT variable in a plant growth experiment is ___.
choices: the amount of sunlight the plant receives
the height of the plant — this is what DEPENDS on the independent variable and is measured
exercises.exp: Dependent variable = what changes as a RESULT of the independent variable — what you measure. Plant height DEPENDS ON time and conditions. It is plotted on the y-axis of a graph.

exercises.question: When plotting a BAR CHART of temperature vs. city, what goes on the X-AXIS?
exercises.exp: On a bar chart, the x-axis shows the categories (cities, independent variable) and the y-axis shows the measured values (temperatures, dependent variable). Categories on x, values on y!

exercises.question: A student calculates the MEAN of five measurements: 12, 14, 13, 15, 11. The mean is ___.
exercises.exp: Mean = sum ÷ number of values = (12+14+13+15+11) ÷ 5 = 65 ÷ 5 = 13. The mean gives the 'average' value — useful for summarising repeated measurements!
